mcqs.q: A cerebrovascular stroke is defined as a focal neurological deficit lasting:
mcqs.explain: A stroke is a sudden focal neurological deficit (from occlusion or rupture) with signs lasting longer than 24 hours.

mcqs.q: A 65-year-old hypertensive develops left-sided weakness and numbness that completely resolves within one hour. The diagnosis is:
mcqs.explain: A focal deficit lasting <60 min that resolves completely within 24 h is a TIA — a warning of future stroke.

mcqs.q: Which type of stroke is the most common?
mcqs.explain: Ischaemic stroke (thrombosis or embolism) accounts for ~80%; haemorrhagic stroke is ~20%.

mcqs.q: An embolic ischaemic stroke is most commonly caused by:
mcqs.explain: Embolic stroke commonly arises from atrial fibrillation, intracardiac thrombus after MI, or infective endocarditis.

mcqs.q: A subarachnoid haemorrhage classically presents with:
opts: Sudden severe headache, vomiting and neck rigidity
mcqs.explain: SAH from a ruptured aneurysm/AVM causes a sudden severe headache, vomiting, neck rigidity and disturbed consciousness.

mcqs.q: A 68-year-old hypertensive develops left-sided weakness; CT brain shows a WHITE (hyperdense) lesion in the right hemisphere. The diagnosis is:
mcqs.explain: A hyperdense (white) lesion on CT indicates fresh blood — a cerebral haemorrhage; an infarct appears dark (hypodense).

mcqs.q: Early in an ISCHAEMIC stroke, the CT brain is often:
opts: Normal (the infarct appears later as a dark area)
mcqs.explain: CT may be normal in the early stages of an ischaemic stroke; the infarct later appears hypodense (dark). MRI is more sensitive early.

mcqs.q: Which speech disturbance can occur in stroke?
mcqs.explain: Stroke can cause dysarthria or aphasia, along with paralysis/paresis, sensory loss, visual loss and facial palsy.

mcqs.q: The simple bedside tool for recognising stroke is:
mcqs.explain: FAST — Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call — is the standard stroke-recognition tool.

mcqs.q: In subarachnoid haemorrhage, which drug helps reduce cerebral vasospasm?
mcqs.explain: Nimodipine, a calcium-channel blocker, reduces intracranial vasospasm after subarachnoid haemorrhage.

mcqs.q: Elective dental treatment after a stroke should ideally be postponed for:
mcqs.explain: The first (non-emergency) dental appointment should not be scheduled until 6 months after the initial stroke; elective care is postponed.

mcqs.q: A 72-year-old with a recent stroke and bulbar palsy needs dental care. The best position is:
mcqs.explain: Treat the patient in a sitting upright position to prevent aspiration of foreign bodies/secretions (impaired gag reflex with bulbar palsy).

mcqs.q: For a stroke patient on warfarin, the INR before dental treatment should be:
mcqs.explain: INR should be between 1.5 and 3.5 for effective coagulation; if below 1.5, consult the physician, and have local haemostatics ready.

mcqs.q: Which antibiotics should be AVOIDED in a patient on warfarin (they raise the INR)?
mcqs.explain: Metronidazole and tetracyclines decrease the effectiveness of warfarin metabolism and can dangerously raise the INR.

mcqs.q: Which analgesic should be AVOIDED in a stroke patient because of the risk of severe hypotension?
mcqs.explain: Opioids are avoided in stroke patients as they may cause severe hypotension; norepinephrine is also avoided (cerebral haemorrhage risk).

mcqs.q: A seizure is best defined as:
opts: A paroxysmal uncontrolled electrical discharge of neurons interrupting normal function
mcqs.explain: A seizure is a paroxysmal uncontrolled electrical discharge of brain neurons, with EEG changes; epilepsy is most prevalent at 5–20 years.

mcqs.q: The difference between a SIMPLE and a COMPLEX partial seizure is:
opts: Simple has no loss of consciousness; complex has impaired awareness
mcqs.explain: Simple partial seizures occur without loss of consciousness; complex partial seizures involve impaired consciousness/awareness.

mcqs.q: Which disorder presents with abnormal movement preceded by an AURA?
mcqs.explain: Tonic-clonic (grand mal) seizures are preceded by an aura (mood change, hallucination), then tonic and clonic phases.

mcqs.q: During the TONIC phase of a grand mal seizure, you would see:
opts: Rigidity, eye-rolling, cyanosis, tongue biting and incontinence
Brief staring with eye blinking only
mcqs.explain: The tonic phase shows limb extension/rigidity, upward eye-roll, cyanosis, teeth clenching, tongue bite, frothing and urinary incontinence.

mcqs.q: A transient weakness AFTER a seizure (post-ictal) is called:
mcqs.explain: Todd's paralysis is post-ictal weakness from neuronal exhaustion, lasting up to 24 hours.

mcqs.q: Absence (petit mal) seizures are characterised by:
opts: Brief 2–10 s staring with no aura and no sequelae, never due to a tumour
A prolonged convulsion with tongue biting
mcqs.explain: Petit mal causes a few seconds of staring/blinking with brief loss of consciousness, no aura/sequelae, from developmental abnormality (never tumours).

mcqs.q: The single most important investigation for diagnosing epilepsy is:
mcqs.explain: The EEG is the most important investigation in epilepsy; CT/MRI exclude structural causes.

mcqs.q: Which antiepileptic drug classically causes gingival overgrowth?
mcqs.explain: Phenytoin causes gingival swelling/overgrowth and coarsening of facial features; large doses cause nystagmus/ataxia.

mcqs.q: Sodium valproate is relevant to dental surgery because it:
opts: Depresses platelet number/function, causing a bleeding tendency
mcqs.explain: Sodium valproate depresses platelet numbers and function, producing a bleeding tendency relevant before surgery.

mcqs.q: Status epilepticus is defined as a seizure lasting:
opts: Longer than 30 minutes (or repeated seizures without regaining consciousness)
mcqs.explain: Status epilepticus is a seizure >30 minutes, or repeated generalised seizures without regaining consciousness — potentially fatal.

mcqs.q: Which IV drug is first-line for status epilepticus?
mcqs.explain: First-line is IV diazepam 10–20 mg (or lorazepam); phenytoin is second-line and phenobarbital third-line.

mcqs.q: If a patient has a seizure in the dental chair, you should first:
opts: Remove instruments, lower the chair and roll the patient onto their side
Put a spoon in the mouth
mcqs.explain: Remove instruments, lower the chair, turn the patient on their side (prevent aspiration), protect from injury and loosen the collar; call EMS if it lasts >5 minutes.

mcqs.q: After a seizure has finished in the dental office, you should:
opts: Place them in the recovery position and not undertake further treatment that day
Send them home alone at once
Give them food and drink immediately
mcqs.explain: Move the patient into the recovery position, do no further treatment that day, keep them until fully recovered, and give nothing to eat/drink until recovered.

mcqs.q: Patients on phenytoin, phenobarbital or carbamazepine have an increased risk of fracture because these drugs:
opts: Alter vitamin D metabolism and clearance
mcqs.explain: These enzyme-inducing antiepileptics alter vitamin D metabolism/clearance, increasing the risk of bone fracture.

mcqs.q: Periodontal (gum) disease has been specifically associated with which stroke subtype?
mcqs.explain: Periodontal disease is associated with ischaemic stroke, so preventive dental care and oral hygiene are emphasised.

saqs.q: Define stroke and TIA, and give the two main stroke types.
saqs.a: Stroke: sudden focal neurological deficit lasting >24 h. TIA: focal deficit <60 min, resolving within 24 h. Types: ischaemic (80%) — thrombosis/embolism; haemorrhagic (20%) — intracerebral/subarachnoid.

saqs.q: How do infarct and haemorrhage appear on CT, and why does it matter?
saqs.a: Haemorrhage = white (hyperdense); infarct = dark (hypodense), often normal early. It matters because thrombolysis helps an infarct but is catastrophic in a bleed.

saqs.q: List the dental precautions for a stroke patient.
saqs.a: Postpone elective care 6 months; short morning visits; treat upright (aspiration); BP ≤140/90; warfarin INR 1.5–3.5 (avoid metronidazole/tetracyclines); low epinephrine; avoid opioids.
Aura (mood change/hallucination) → tonic phase (rigidity, eye-roll, cyanosis, tongue bite, incontinence) → clonic phase (rhythmic jerking) → post-ictal (confusion, ± Todd's paralysis).

saqs.q: Contrast absence seizures with focal seizures, and name relevant drugs.
saqs.a: Absence: childhood, 2–10 s staring, no aura/sequelae, never tumour (ethosuximide/valproate). Focal: simple (no LOC) or complex (impaired awareness, automatisms) (carbamazepine/valproate).

saqs.q: Define status epilepticus and outline its management.
saqs.a: Seizure >30 min or repeated seizures without regaining consciousness. Manage ABC + IV diazepam/lorazepam first-line, then phenytoin, then phenobarbital; intubation/anaesthesia if it persists.

saqs.q: What should the dental team do during and after a seizure in the chair?
saqs.a: During: remove instruments, lower chair, side position, protect from injury, loosen collar; EMS if >5 min. After: recovery position, no further treatment that day, keep until fully recovered.
